f1.quote: Molecular-dynamics simulations varied Nb, Ta, Ti, or Zr individually among 0, 10, 20, and 30 at.%, with the compositional difference assigned to Hf, producing 13 unique alloys.

f2.quote: The study calculated tensile strength, elastic modulus, elongation, fracture evolution, and optimized-composition thermal behavior; Nb10, Ta10, and Ti0 were subsequently tested from 300 to 1200 K, and their thermal expansion was calculated during heating.

f3.quote: Uniaxial tension was applied along z at 1 × 10^8 s^-1, primarily at 300 K.

f4.quote: Thermal tests covered 300–1200 K in 300 K increments; thermal-expansion simulations used a heating rate of 0.02 K/fs.

f5.quote: At low Nb or Ta addition, substitutional solutes disrupt the lattice and form a strengthening solid solution that impedes dislocation motion.

f6.quote: Elevated temperature increases lattice vibrations and facilitates dislocation migration, reducing strength and stiffness.

f7.quote: Tensile failure proceeds by bond breaking and shear localization near 45° to the loading direction, producing cup-and-cone-type ductile fracture.

f8.quote: Relative to the equimolar alloy, reducing Nb or Ta from 20% to 10% is expected to increase ultimate tensile strength and elastic modulus, whereas increasing either to 30% is expected to reduce both.

f11.quote: Ti and Zr variations are expected to show the opposite, nonmonotonic trend: an initial decline upon addition followed by recovery at higher content.

f12.quote: The optimized alloys are expected to lose strength and stiffness as temperature increases.
